overview: Adena is an archaeological name for related material and ceremonial traditions in the Ohio River region. It is not the recorded self-name of one tribe or kingdom. Local histories differ, and the label should not erase the people and communities whose work created the surviving objects and earthworks.

periods.title: Early Woodland traditions in Ohio
periods.summary: One Ohio chronology places Adena traditions around 800 BCE to 100 CE. These approximate boundaries vary with regional sequences and archaeological definitions.

periods.title: An imported map date needing correction
periods.summary: One imported record labels this interval Adena, but the archaeological chronology belongs much earlier. This map label does not establish an Adena state or a newly founded culture in 1492.

items.text: Excavated from a Chillicothe burial in 1901, the Adena Pipe depicts a human figure carved in Ohio pipestone. Ear ornaments, a loincloth and a feather bustle make the hollow smoking implement a detailed sculpture.

The figure’s large ear ornaments helped archaeologists interpret similar objects found around other burials. Yet none of the people excavated from this mound had those ornaments. The image can illuminate ways of wearing objects without proving that the person buried with the pipe dressed exactly like its figure.

A surviving textile from the central grave has fine yarns worked in alternate-pair twining. Researchers considered the yarn likely to be plant bast fibre. This small fragment preserves evidence of skilled fibre preparation and weaving, while its identification remains more cautious than naming a particular plant species.

Tree bark preserved from the same grave was identified as black locust. Later radiocarbon work produced different ages for bark and textile. An older garment or shroud kept as an heirloom is one proposed explanation. The results date organic material and require interpretation; they do not give the stone pipe a direct laboratory date.

At Cowan Creek Mound, excavators found charred goosefoot seeds and squash rind on the floor of a circular structure, associated with remnants of a woven container. The squash supported an inference of cultivation. The original botanist regarded the goosefoot seeds as wild, a useful reminder that collected and cultivated foods could occur together.

Paired postmolds beneath Cowan Creek Mound reveal a circular timber structure. Initially called a dwelling, it was later interpreted as a place for mortuary ceremonies before mound construction. The physical post pattern is secure evidence of a building; choosing between household and ceremonial uses requires the wider context.

The National Park Service describes communities living for extended periods near waterways while combining gardening with hunting and gathering. Nuts, berries and seed-bearing plants complemented cultivated foods. This mixed economy required familiarity with seasonal habitats as well as the practical work of growing, collecting and storing food.

Pottery provided containers for gathered plants and other stored food. The same regional account describes increasingly durable and decorated vessels, alongside timber shelters covered with plant material and earth. Making containers and maintaining homes were important technical activities, even though monuments are more conspicuous in the surviving landscape.

sections.title: Earthworks and the limits of evidence

items.text: Grave Creek Mound in present-day West Virginia grew through successive construction stages, approximately 250 to 150 BCE. Burials at different levels support the sequence. Repeated additions show a monument changing through use; the surviving mound does not represent one afternoon of construction or necessarily one ruler’s commission.

The 1838 investigation of Grave Creek used tunnels and a shaft rather than modern controlled excavation. An inscribed stone reportedly found there has never been authenticated and is disputed by specialists. It cannot securely establish an Adena writing system or contact with a distant civilization.

Greber explains that sites labelled Adena and Hopewell overlap in time. Combining objects from many regions into one checklist can conceal local differences. Studying individual valleys and site sequences gives a better basis for discussing changing ceremonies and craftsmanship than treating these labels as rival kingdoms with clean borders.

ending.text: Adena and Hopewell categories overlap as local practices change. This is not a documented conquest or fall of a kingdom, and the ending of an archaeological classification is not evidence that its communities vanished.
